episode_title: A Deep Dive Into the Indian Military

stories.summary: Amit raves about Perun, a pseudonymous YouTuber Ajay had introduced him to during prep for their 5.5-hour Ukraine episode. Perun is an economist who makes long, dense PowerPoint videos with no production values, no on-camera presence, no books behind him, and no media brand — yet has built an audience of nearly half a million subscribers. His videos run an hour or more, are crammed with words and bullet points, and break every conventional rule of YouTube.
stories.insight: A repudiation of credentialism and shallowness simultaneously. You don't need MIT/IIT/NYT cachet, and you don't need to dumb things down — what wins is depth, sense-making, and content that respects the audience's hunger for understanding.

stories.topic: Gell-Mann Amnesia (and Perun's Surprising Resistance to It)
stories.summary: Amit explains the Gell-Mann Amnesia effect — Crichton's coinage for Murray Gell-Mann's observation that we read a newspaper, find rubbish in the field we know, then turn the page and trust everything else. When Amit, who has done multiple Indian-defence episodes, watched Perun's video on Indian defence, he expected to catch the usual elementary errors a foreign expert would make. Instead Perun's understanding was rock-solid — better than many Indians whose actual job it is to know this.
stories.insight: Gell-Mann amnesia is a useful epistemic trip-wire: what we know firsthand exposes the bullshit elsewhere. The rare creator who survives that test in your home domain has earned trust on subjects you can't verify.

stories.topic: The Snake Without a Tail (Asking for the Wrong Specs)
stories.summary: Perun's metaphor for Indian defence procurement, which Amit narrates from memory: imagine you're a foreign defence firm. India hands you a budget for a single room, then asks you to build a township that flies to space — fully advanced, with an Indian partner who must own at least 51%, all your IP transferred, you bear 100% of any risk, and the requirements may keep changing throughout. Perun's punchline: the army is asking for 2030 tech, being told it can have 2010 tech, says "no, fuck it" — and ends up with 1940 tech. Cue 'a slow clap.'
stories.insight: When a procurement process couples impossible requirements, hostile commercial terms, and changing specs, the rational response from the world's best vendors is to walk away — leaving the buyer stuck with what nobody else wants. The dream of self-reliance becomes the trap of obsolescence.

stories.topic: The MiG-21 Tragedy (and the Self-Reliance Body Count)
stories.summary: MiG-21s are 1960s aircraft. India should have phased them out 30 years ago; we are still flying them, and experienced pilots — extraordinary human capital — still die in their crashes. Ajai Shukla and Devesh Kapur have documented 2,374 IAF crashes and 1,305 pilots killed. The decades-long indigenous LCA project, which Ajay personally benefited from in 1983 when its R&D funded a CFD lab he worked in, has now finally flown — with foreign engines.
stories.insight: The cost of forced self-reliance is paid in the lives of trained pilots and in decades of obsolete equipment. By the time a 30-year indigenous program reaches the runway, the rest of the world has moved a generation ahead.

stories.topic: The Pension Negotiation That Was Lost in Transit
stories.summary: In the early days of the National Pension System under Vajpayee, Ajay was deputed by S. Narayan in the Finance Ministry to negotiate with the Army, Navy and Air Force on how NPS would be implemented for the military. There was an oral agreement at senior leadership across all three services. Then the UPA came in in 2004; the CPI(M) blocked NPS; pensions was moved (wrongly, in Ajay's view) from DEA to DFS; institutional memory evaporated. By the time NPS rolled out, the military piece was forgotten — and we ended up with OROP, the exact opposite of what had been agreed.
stories.insight: Reform happens in moments. When the moment passes — through political turnover, bureaucratic reshuffles, lost institutional memory — the careful agreements vanish, and you get the negation of what was nearly achieved. State capacity is in part the capacity to remember.

stories.topic: The Aeronautical Development Agency Funded Ajay's College Lab
stories.summary: Ajay started college in 1983 and was the immediate beneficiary of a computational fluid dynamics lab at his institution funded by ADA — the agency set up by the IAF to do the deep R&D leading up to the LCA. He uses this to mark how old the LCA project is: a man who is now a senior public-policy thinker was a young undergraduate when the project's R&D was already in motion.
stories.insight: When a single weapons-development program spans a person's entire adult career and still hasn't delivered global state-of-the-art equipment, you are looking at a structural failure of strategy, not bad luck.

stories.summary: Reflecting on the quiet, professional, clinical army of Sam Manekshaw, Y. B. Chavan and Indira Gandhi in 1971, Amit slips in a play on Chavan's name: 'one could say that Mr. Chavan was a man also given not just to military affairs but metaphysics, because he would always be thinking, why be Chavan?' (Y. B. = 'why be'.)
stories.insight: A throwaway pun that doubles as a reminder that the 1971 generation of Indian leaders were thinkers and questioners, not just operators — exactly the texture of leadership the army has lost.

stories.topic: France and Germany — From Centuries of Killing to Driving to Work Across the Border
stories.summary: France and Germany killed each other in the Napoleonic Wars, in 1870, in 1914, and in 1945 — four wars across a century. After 1945, they finally sorted it out. Today, people living in France wake up, drive into Germany, go to work, and don't have to show a passport at the border.
stories.insight: The European Union is the proof of concept that civilisational hostility can be ended through institutions and treaties. The ideal is not 'win the next war' but 'make the next war impossible' — and history shows this is achievable, even between the bitterest enemies.

stories.topic: Ten Percent of Ukraine's Army Is Women — and the Sniper Insight
stories.summary: Ajay notes that ten percent of Ukraine's serving army today is women, and pushes back on the macho image of soldiering. Women, he argues, make great sniper gunners specifically because the temperament the role demands — quiet, clinical, calm, patient, emotionally stable — is exactly what good sniping requires. The hyper-masculine 'blood-curdling scream' image is the opposite of what wins modern wars.
stories.insight: Modern war is won by traits the macho stereotype actively suppresses. A correct theory of military effectiveness is also a correct theory of inclusion — the people who score lowest on bellicosity may score highest on the skills the battlefield actually requires.

stories.topic: Indian Soldier Recruitment — The 15km Run in a Village
stories.summary: A 'filtration criterion' Ajay reports reading about for Indian military hiring: thousands of young men gather at a village; they are made to run 15 kilometres; the top 1% by time get shortlisted. Ajay's reaction: you can take almost any person and train them to military levels of fitness — biceps are trivial. What you cannot train is the brain. The choke point of a modern army is brainpower, and we are filtering for legs.
stories.insight: If you select for the wrong trait, you optimize the entire pipeline against the trait that actually matters. A modern army needs people who can read English manuals, play chess and poker simultaneously, and creatively misuse Western kit — not people who can run 15km in a field.

stories.summary: When the war started, Ukrainians built what Ajay and Amit have called an 'Uber for artillery' — a small-team software innovation that allowed rapid coordination of fire across the battlefield, the kind of thing a normal military bureaucracy could never have produced. The Ukrainians have also been tearing up the software of Western equipment and rebuilding it, finding new applications for tools that the original makers never imagined.
stories.insight: The decisive military advantage now goes to the small, empowered, creative, subversive team that rewrites its own tools on the fly. Top-down agricultural armies cannot do this — and that is why they are losing the new century of war.

stories.topic: Poland Bought a Korean Tank Instead of an Abrams
stories.summary: Faced with a possible Russian invasion if Ukraine falls, Poland chose not to buy the German Leopard 2 or American M1 Abrams. They bought a South Korean tank — one notch behind global state of the art, but affordable enough to field thousands. They negotiated deep partnerships with Korea: shared R&D, shared manufacturing, equity, royalties on future global sales.
stories.insight: A pragmatic poor- or middle-budget country buys one notch behind the frontier and amplifies through scale, rather than chasing an unaffordable best-in-class. Self-reliance is the wrong objective; scale and sensible specs are the right ones.

stories.topic: More Sukhoi-30s Fly Over India Than Over Russia
stories.summary: An aside Amit picks up from Perun's video: there are now more Sukhoi-30 fighters flying over India than over Russia. A purchasing decision rooted in Cold War alignment has, decades later, made India the largest operator of an aircraft that even its country of origin uses less.
stories.insight: Procurement decisions are extraordinarily sticky. A choice made for geopolitical reasons in one decade locks the country into an entire equipment ecosystem (parts, training, doctrine) for a generation — even after the geopolitics has flipped.

stories.topic: A Free Corps in Weimar Germany — How Veterans Become Brownshirts
stories.summary: After the First World War, German veterans came back into an informal organization called the Free Corps. They concentrated all the toxic right-wing nationalist energy — strong-man values, intolerance, willingness to take to the streets and engage in violence. That was the raw material around which the Nazi Party was built. The brownshirts were drawn from many Free Corps elements. Then that society, led by Hitler, fed back into the military project of conquering the world — which ended badly for Germany.
stories.insight: There is a two-way feedback loop between militarism in the army and militarism in the society. Keeping the army in the barracks (a Nehruvian achievement Ajay credits explicitly) is not a courtesy to the army — it is the only way to keep the polity from being eaten by the army's worst tendencies.

recommendations.context: Pseudonymous Australian ex-military economist who makes hour-plus PowerPoint videos on defence economics and geopolitics, including a recent deep dive on Indian defence.
recommendations.reason: The whole episode is built off Perun's video on Indian defence. He is the model of expertise without credentials, depth without dumbing-down, and a sense-maker for both Ukraine and Indian defence.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's online writing course; registration was open for the Feb 2024 cohort at the time of this episode.
recommendations.reason: Self-recommended at the top of the show notes — the closest in-house product to the show's own ethos of clear thinking and clear expression.

core_ideas.concept: Three-Step Military Strategy: Threats → Cost-Efficient Force Design → Incremental Implementation
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's structured frame for fundamental military strategy. Step 1: identify and write down the actual threats facing the country, recognising that they evolve (China at 5x GDP poses different problems than China at 1x). Step 2: design a cost-efficient force that addresses those threats — 'cost-efficient' is non-negotiable because a democracy cannot afford a militaristic-state share of GDP, and infinite budgets would solve any problem. Step 3: implement incrementally, recognising path dependence — you cannot tear down an existing force and rebuild from scratch (a back-of-envelope: replacing all equipment at half-percent-of-GDP-per-year × 20-year lifespans = 20% of GDP, which nobody will ever fund). Re-engineer your existing T-72s with new electronics rather than whining about them.
core_ideas.quote: We are not here to whine about the decisions made by people before you. Standing where we are, what are the incremental pathways that we can adopt today?

core_ideas.concept: Foundational Processes: HR, Contracting, Finance, Checks-and-Balances
core_ideas.explanation: From Kelkar and Shah's *In Service of the Republic*. Four cross-cutting capabilities that afflict every Indian public-policy field — health, defence, finance, monetary policy, intelligence, judiciary. The vertical thinker (the 'health expert') believes their problems are unique to their sector; the horizontal thinker recognises the same plumbing problems everywhere. (1) HR — how do you hire, fire, promote, measure performance? (2) Government contracting — almost everything works better contracted out, but the state needs the capability to procure, manage contracts, and pay vendors on time. (3) Finance — budgets that create accountability and pay private vendors when promised. (4) Checks and balances on coercive power. Defence is just one more domain where these four are broken.
core_ideas.quote: Disciplinary boundaries create an emphasis. If you're a health [expert], you verticalize: I'm a polio person, or I'm an HIV person. This is the most useless way to do health.

core_ideas.concept: The Critic Shortage in Strategic Thinking
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's diagnosis of why India keeps failing on strategy: the absence of self-appointed long-term communities of thinkers. In the UK, US, and Germany there are recognisable national-security and economic-strategy communities that work across elections and own the 25-year view. In India, people 'play for their time on the watch' — somebody promoted at 59 plays for one year. There was a brief intellectual flowering in the Narasimha Rao / Vajpayee / Jaswant Singh / Manmohan Singh continuity that questioned India's pro-Soviet alignment, but it didn't go far enough. Today the Indian Foreign Service and military bureaucracy are still defending a non-aligned, prickly, pro-global-South stance that no longer maps to where India's economic interests, elite educational pathways, and strategic interests actually lie.

core_ideas.concept: The Pessimism of Path Dependence: Inherited Military, Constructed Diplomacy
core_ideas.explanation: In 1947 India inherited a world-class military: a force trained at Sandhurst, blooded in two world wars, with eighty-seven thousand of its members killed in WWII. What India did *not* inherit was a foreign-policy capability — that had to be built from scratch, and Ajay argues Nehru and Krishna Menon did a poor job. The result: India has spent decades doing speeches at the UN instead of negotiations. Indian foreign policy starts with 'strategic autonomy,' which is to say 'my domestic policy is not up for discussion' — exactly the wrong opening move for diplomacy, which is the art of mutual modification of domestic policy.

core_ideas.concept: Diplomacy as the Outer Layer; Military Power as What Diplomacy Failed
core_ideas.explanation: The military capability has to be there — you must have the big stick — but it is most efficient when used least, both because killing is morally wrong and because it is expensive. Diplomacy's job is to achieve the country's interests so that the stick rarely needs to be swung. WWI, Hitler's invasion of Poland, and Russia's invasion of Ukraine were each fundamentally failures of diplomacy. Today's diplomacy is doing the heavy lifting of warning Xi Jinping not to invade Taiwan; if it succeeds, it is the triumph of diplomacy. Treaties and coalitions also reduce defence costs — going alone is a needless expensive choice when partnerships allow countries to risk-insure each other.
core_ideas.quote: It was the failure of Indian foreign policy that created the conditions where the United States was solidly aligned with Pakistan in 1971.

core_ideas.concept: Why Self-Reliant Defence Procurement Cannot Work for Anyone but the US
core_ideas.explanation: Only the United States can plausibly do isolated, self-reliant development of global state-of-the-art systems at acceptable cost. Three reasons: (1) the deepest private R&D ecosystem in the world (DARPA, universities, private firms); (2) export scale — they make thousands of fighters, not hundreds, which crashes unit costs; (3) they actually don't really do self-reliance — DoD contracts flow to Japan, Israel, and Europe, with the Italian-Spanish-French drone programs, German-British fighters, Korean-Polish tank deals. Everyone else is doing multi-country partnerships. India's LCA project, started before Ajay went to college, finally flew with foreign engines. The lesson: pick one notch behind the global frontier, integrate into global supply chains, and amplify with scale.

core_ideas.concept: Toxic Masculinity Doesn't Win Modern Wars
core_ideas.explanation: The Bollywood/Telugu-cinema image of the army — bellicose, fanatical, masculine, blood-curdling-screams, agricultural workforce — is the opposite of what wins modern wars. Ever since Joan of Arc, fanatics don't win wars. Modern war is a complex thinking project: chess + poker, mind games, strategy, logistics, advanced weapons, TTP (techniques, tactics, procedures), morale, training, equipment, teamwork, creativity, flexibility, adaptation under fire. The 1971 army of Manekshaw, Y. B. Chavan, and Indira Gandhi was a quiet, clinical, professional army. The bellicose tone is a recent populist phenomenon, and it's exactly the wrong DNA for an army that wants to win.
core_ideas.quote: Wars are won by thinking, by cleverness, by creativity, by flexibility, by teamwork. It's not a game of blood-curdling screams by an agricultural workforce.

core_ideas.concept: Hire for Brain, Train the Biceps
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's heretical proposal for Indian military recruitment: paper number one is your ELO on chess.com; paper number two is poker, because the battlefield (unlike chess) is partly invisible. Then teach them biceps and a little masculinity afterward — those are the easy parts. The choke point of a modern army is brainpower, the ability to read English manuals, work with complex global equipment, creatively misuse Western kit, and improvise under fire. The gold standard is what's already true in the IAF and Navy: small-headcount, highly trained, English-fluent, technologically adept forces. The Army is still essentially an agricultural workforce, and modernizing it is the central challenge.

core_ideas.concept: The 'New Army' Path to Modernization (Battalion Tactical Groups)
core_ideas.explanation: When the Russians wanted to modernize their old, top-down, agricultural USSR-style army (which the Indian Army resembles), they didn't try to reform the old beast. They built parallel — small thousand-person 'battalion tactical groups' with new manuals, new processes, new doctrine, deep integration with air and naval assets, and an explicit cultural mandate to be unlike the old army. Ajay's proposal for India: phase down the old army slowly over decades while building new modern formations alongside, infused with Air Force and Navy culture, doing combined arms with drones, electronic warfare, and infantry integration. Don't try to reform the giant directly — build a new culture next to it.

core_ideas.concept: Defence Economics: One Notch Behind the Frontier, Plus Scale
core_ideas.explanation: Two principles for poor-country defence procurement. (1) Pitch yourself one notch behind global state of the art — Poland bought Korean tanks rather than M1 Abrams; an Indian garment factory uses ten-year-old equipment, not European state-of-the-art. Don't whine, just make do. (2) Scale, scale, scale — fewer SKUs, more units of each, integrated into global supply chains, possibly exported. The chess analogy: adding up the value of pieces (queen=9, rook=5, pawn=1) is the most stupid way to assess a position. The same is true of equipment lists. Israel in 1967, outgunned in equipment by every Arab opponent put together, won the Six-Day War. Russia in 2022, vastly outgunning Ukraine on paper, has not.

core_ideas.concept: Nuclear Deterrence Has Broken the Reform-Through-Defeat Loop
core_ideas.explanation: Historically, states that did a poor job of defence got slapped around in war, lost territory and population, and were forced into a wave of reform. India followed exactly this pattern: defeat in 1962 woke up Nehru and others to deep reforms, which became the raw material for better outcomes in 1965 and the victory of 1971. Each crisis between 1947 and 1999 — '47-48, '62, '65, '71, Kargil — exposed weaknesses and triggered reform. But since 1999, mutual nuclear deterrence between India, China, and Pakistan has frozen the major-war loop. So today's accumulating military weaknesses go untested. If a real conventional war breaks out — Ukraine-style — many things may turn out to be badly broken in ways nobody currently sees.
core_ideas.quote: If you play an old game, then you go through 1947, 48, 65, 71, 99 — each of those exposes lack of capabilities and initiates calls for reform.

core_ideas.concept: The Optimism: Knowledge Comes Before Reform
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's counterweight to the pessimism: for the first time in India's history, we are developing a real domestic literature on law, public administration, state capacity, and reform — and a new cadre of people who think with it. The kindling is being laid. Reform begins as ideas; only then does implementation become possible. Many of the things this episode discusses could not have been done before, not because nobody wanted to, but because the knowledge wasn't there and the people weren't there. That has changed. In an open society, ideas matter — and in an open India, those ideas will eventually find their way into practice.
core_ideas.quote: First comes the idea. Then there is a possibility of implementation. So in some ways, the kindling is being laid.

core_ideas.concept: Demographic Dividend Wasted: Old Army, Young Country
core_ideas.explanation: India's structural advantage — massive young population — should mean a young army. The US Marines have an average age between 21 and 25; the Indian Army averages 32-34. The reason is structural: India hires for life. Fifteen-year minimum contracts that stretch into 20-25 year careers, then 50 years of pensions (now 23% of the defence budget, up from 12% in 2008). Foreign armies use short-term contracts with selective extensions. Agnipath tried to fix this — five-year contracts with only 15-25% retained, severance instead of pensions for the rest — and triggered nationwide protests because Indians think of the army as 'Kurya for life.' The structural reform is necessary but politically nearly impossible.

The pension story is its own catastrophe. Pension share of the defence budget has nearly doubled since 2008, crowding out modernization. Of $47 billion in defence spending in 2023, only ~$3.7 billion went to actual modernization. NPS (the National Pension System) was almost extended to the military in the early NPS years — Ajay personally led the negotiations and got service-leadership buy-in — but institutional memory was lost in the UPA transition, NPS-for-military was forgotten, and OROP (One Rank One Pension) became the political reality instead. OROP is the exact opposite of NPS in fiscal logic. The military pension bill will only get larger from here, and the modernisation crunch only worse.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on Perun's pretensions to slick production values: 'There is no slick video production. There is no great video editing. It is laughably dense.' His verdict on the boring multi-hour format: 'It's really emboldening for the boring old fogies like you and me who are the purveyors of this kind of dreary multi-hour content.' Amit's reply: 'Speak for yourself, Ajai Shah. You know I am not boring and dreary and old.'
Amit's pun on Y. B. Chavan: 'one could say that Mr. Chavan was a man also given not just to military affairs but metaphysics, because he would always be thinking, why be Chavan?'

Ajay's metaphor for Indian defence procurement: imagine you're a foreign vendor, India hands you the budget for a single room, then asks you to build a township that flies to space, with mandatory Indian partners, IP transfer, 100% liability, and the requirements may keep changing. Perun's punchline: the army wants 2030 tech, is offered 2010 tech, says 'no, fuck it' — and ends up with 1940 tech. 'This calls for, as Perun says, a slow clap.'

Amit on the sectoral myopia of the political conversation: a healthcare expert says 'oh healthcare, you need to fix XYZ; defence, you need to fix ABC; or in so-and-so department you need to fix... I'm trying to think of three more letters... whatever, RST.'

Ajay on calling for ideal Indian recruits: 'You want Vaishnav levels of brain power in the military. I mean, he's a wimp, he doesn't have any biceps. Adding biceps is trivial.' (Vaishnav Vyas is the show's videographer.)

Ajay on phasing out the old army: 'It's a bit jugaad, but get on that long trajectory of downsizing — it's like a new pension system. There is an old pension system; it will phase out slowly, bit by bit, it will come to an [end].'
Amit on the Indian Navy being the underexplored service: 'None of us know much about the Indian Navy given the amount of naval-gazing we [do].'
Amit on the long view: 'Both of us are playing the long game, but as your hero John Maynard Keynes once said, in the long run we are all dead.'
Amit's parting note to viewers: 'Watch all our previous videos. Watch Perun's video. Just watch videos all day. The world is going to hell. Just watch videos.'

Ajay on his standing reading list: 'I have 20 recommendations, which is — everybody, gentle reader, should read books on the Second World War. It doesn't matter which books you read.' His advice: read at least two, and once you're past n=2, read Hanson's *The Second World Wars*.

Ajay teasing Amit's increasing pessimism about government reform: 'How conservative you have become. This is a country where customs duties went from three hundred fifty percent to fifteen percent. Anything is possible.'
Gell-Mann Amnesia — Michael Crichton's coinage after Murray Gell-Mann's observation that we trust newspapers on every topic except the one we know personally, where we know it's all wrong.
'Adapt, improvise, overcome' — the US Marines adage Ajay invokes for the kind of small-team creativity modern warfare demands.
Clausewitz: 'War is politics by other means' — invoked by Amit to motivate the diplomacy-as-prevention chapter.
Nitin Pai's running argument that India's economic interests today lie squarely with the West — invoked by Ajay against the bureaucratic legacy of non-alignment and global-South posturing.
Narasimha Rao to Vajpayee in 1996, on handing over power: 'Saamagri tayyar hai' — the materials for the nuclear test are ready. Vajpayee told this story after Rao's death in the early 2000s.
Manmohan Singh's 'I'd rather not be Prime Minister than not get this done' stance during the Indo-US nuclear deal during UPA-1 — invoked as the model of an existential reformer's commitment.

The Free Corps and the brownshirts — Weimar Germany's veterans' organisation that became the recruitment pool for the Nazi Party, used as the canonical example of how militarism in society and militarism in the army feed each other.

'Sense maker' — Amit's favoured term (alongside 'curator') for the kind of high-trust analyst (Perun on Ukraine, Lawrence Freedman on strategy, Eric Topol on COVID, Yascha Mounk on illiberal democracy) we use social media to follow rather than to argue with.
